items.title: CLIC: Closed-Loop Intent Consistency for Securing LLM-Driven Control in Open RAN
items.abstract: With the progressive capabilities of large language models (LLMs), researchers are finding ways to integrate them into the control loops of Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) to enable slicing and resource management through user intents. However, integration of LLMs in the O-RAN control loop via the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) makes the system vulnerable to \textit{runtime prompt injection threats}, which manipulate control decisions without violating interface authentication, and \textit{residual virtual prompt injection (VPI)} attacks that plant trigger mechanisms to silently steer the behaviour during fine-tuning. Existing studies address only the runtime threat and do not enforce consistency across the full control path, i.e. from the certified A1 intent, through the multi-step LLM trajectory, to the final E2 action. We propose a closed-loop intent-consistency layer (CLIC) that jointly mitigates both threats. The proposed CLIC defines a formal consistency score using a small quantized language model, which is deployed as a Non-RT rApp for model-integrity certification along with a Near-RT xApp for runtime enforcement. We implement CLIC on the OpenAI Cellular (OAIC) platform and evaluate it under domain-adapted JailbreakBench, AdvBench, and VPI workloads. The experimental results show that the proposed CLIC reduces the attack success rate from 0.92 to 0.29 and residual VPI attacks from 0.37 to 0.04, while improving isolation and fairness at slightly higher latency costs, i.e. approximately 27 ms.

items.title: Clinical Phenotypes, Machine‐Learning Risk Stratification and Treatment Outcomes of Constipation in Stroke Patients Receiving Enteral Nutrition: A Retrospective Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Stroke-related complications and frequent feeding interruptions often compromise nutritional intake, making enteral nutrition (EN) a cornerstone therapy to improve nutritional status and support recovery. Nevertheless, constipation is highly prevalent and clinically consequential among stroke patients receiving EN, particularly in critically ill populations, where enteral nutrition-associated constipation can impede rehabilitation, increase complications and prolong intensive care unit (ICU) stay. AIM: This study aimed to explore potentially important determinants of enteral nutrition-associated constipation (ENAC) in patients with stroke using artificial intelligence approaches, characterise relevant clinical subgroups, compare internally validated machine-learning models and examine how the temporal availability of candidate predictors may influence model performance. STUDY DESIGN: Clinical data from patients admitted to a neurological intensive care unit between December 2019 and December 2023 were retrospectively analysed. K-means clustering was used to identify clinical subgroups. Six algorithms-logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting tree, XGBoost, LightGBM and Table PFN-3-were compared under temporally restricted and expanded retrospective feature frameworks using five repeats of nested five-fold cross-validation. Performance was assessed using ROC-AUC, average precision, Brier score, calibration and decision-curve analysis. Treatment outcomes were summarised descriptively. RESULTS: Among 362 patients, 233 (64.4%) had documented constipation. Table PFN-3 achieved the highest discrimination in both frameworks. The temporally restricted model yielded a ROC-AUC of 0.629 (95% CI 0.567-0.689), whereas the expanded retrospective model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.771 (95% CI 0.715-0.820), average precision of 0.857, Brier score of 0.177 and calibration slope of 0.965. The ROC-AUC increased by 0.142 (95% CI 0.090-0.201) after full-hospitalisation information was included. K-means clustering retained three subgroups (K = 3; silhouette coefficient = 0.108), with constipation frequencies of 67.35%, 56.98% and 88.89% in Clusters 0, 1 and 2, respectively. Among evaluable patients, observed relief was 80.3% with glycerin enema, 60.0% with lactulose, 72.7% with combination treatment and 65.7% with neither treatment; these treatment comparisons were descriptive. CONCLUSIONS: Table PFN-3 achieved the strongest internally validated performance, with the expanded retrospective framework combining good discrimination, strong precision-recall performance and close calibration. The 0.142 increase in ROC-AUC after completed hospital-course variables were incorporated quantifies the substantial discriminative information that emerges as hospitalisation evolves. Together with the distinct clinical phenotypes and descriptive treatment findings, these results establish a clinically relevant framework for trajectory-aware bowel monitoring and provide a clear rationale for developing dynamic, time-updated prediction models. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: By integrating machine-learning benchmarking, clinical phenotyping and observed treatment outcomes, this study identifies prolonged, treatment-intensive hospital trajectories as a particularly high-burden constipation phenotype and demonstrates that classification performance changes materially as hospital-course information accumulates. These findings support structured reassessment of bowel risk during neurological intensive care rather than reliance on a single static evaluation and provide a practical rationale for future dynamic monitoring tools.

items.title: Close the Gap or Widen It? AI, Equity and Learning at the Weakest Link
items.abstract: Generative AI could be the most powerful equaliser in the history of education, putting a patient, personalised tutor within reach of every child. It could equally widen the gap between advantaged and disadvant‐ aged learners, because new technologies usually reach those with re‐ sources first and those without last, if at all. This article draws on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside data on connectivity, refugee education, aid and AI develop‐ ment policy. It argues that the outcome will not be decided by the techno‐ logy but by deliberate choices, and that leaving AI to markets and chance will produce the worse outcome. It identifies four layers of the AI divide: access, skilled guidance, language and culture, and recognition of what learners achieve. It then examines the weakest link in global education, learners in crisis and displacement, where 5.8 million refugee children were out of school in 2025 and international aid fell by nearly a quarter in a single year. It reviews approaches that work where power, connectivity and funding cannot be assumed, including offline platforms, AI delivered through basic phones, support for community teachers and portable, re‐ cognised certificates, along with their risks. It proposes a six-question equity test for any AI decision in education.

items.title: Co-Creating a Humane Trading Architecture: Enterprise, Innovation and the Bangladesh–European Union Economic Partnership — A Research Paper on Market Measurement, Digital Sovereignty and Phased Integration
items.abstract: Bangladesh's impending transition from least-developed-country status and the initialling of a Framework Agreement on Comprehensive Partnership and Cooperation with the European Union open a structured opportunity to redesign the bilateral economic relationship. This paper develops the concept of a humane trading architecture in which enterprise competitiveness and innovation capacity function as the principal transmission mechanisms between preferential market access and structural transformation. It integrates multidimensional market-measurement tools (the Economic Vulnerability Index and the Environmental Performance Index), mild-form transaction authentication and data validation for small and medium enterprise trade finance, sovereign computational capacity (including a Bangla large language model embedded in digital public infrastructure), and post-quantum readiness for trade finance. Drawing on comparative lessons from the EU–Vietnam Free Trade Agreement and EU–India negotiations, the paper specifies five negotiating redlines, co-creation pathways in food, fuel and finance, and a three-phase roadmap calibrated to the current United Nations graduation schedule and the pending request for a preparatory extension. The resulting framework preserves strategic autonomy while extending economic franchise to domestic firms and workers. Personal academic views only.

items.title: CoFiBreak: A Coarse-to-Fine Diversity Reward for Effective Multi-Turn Jailbreak
items.abstract: Automated red teaming trains an attacker large language model (LLM) to elicit harmful responses from a victim LLM, but reinforcement learning can collapse attackers onto a narrow set of prompts when attack success is the only reward. Such a collapse of attack diversity can bias safety evaluation toward repeatedly testing near-duplicate attack patterns rather than the underlying harmful intents. Existing methods often trade off attack success or inference cost for greater content or strategy diversity. We propose CoFiBreak, a coarse-to-fine diversity reward for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that improves attack diversity while preserving strong attack effectiveness and low inference cost. The coarse reward broadens which strategies the attacker uses by encouraging strategies underrepresented within each GRPO group, while the fine reward broadens how those strategies are realized by discouraging reuse of the same personas, framings, and output formats after harmful-intent information is removed from prompt embeddings. Diversity rewards apply only to attacks that already exceed an effectiveness threshold, so diversity cannot be gained through ineffective attacks. Since both rewards are computed only during training, CoFiBreak also retains inference efficiency. Trained with Llama3.1-8B-Instruct as the victim, CoFiBreak discovers 1.6-2.0x as many distinct successful fine-grained strategies as the strongest baseline across frontier victims on HarmBench. It reaches 98.8% ASR@10 (attack success rate with 10 generations per intent) on AdvBench with the highest diversity score among all compared methods, which is 2.1x that of the strongest-attacking baseline. The resulting attacks transfer to unseen frontier LLMs, reaching 71.0% ASR@10 on AdvBench with the unseen victim Claude-Opus-4.6. The code will be released.

items.title: Cognitive abilities and trust calibration: Understanding individual differences in automation trust dynamics
items.abstract: Individual differences in cognitive abilities may influence how people form and adjust trust in automated systems, yet the mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. This study investigated how three foundational cognitive abilities - working memory (WM), attention control (AC), and fluid intelligence (Gf) - shape trust dynamics, particularly focusing on trust decline and recovery after automation failures. Participants (N = 111) completed cognitive tests measuring WM, AC, and Gf before performing a dual-task paradigm where they monitored an automated memory aid exhibiting varying reliability levels (100%-65%-100%) while completing an arithmetic task. Results revealed that WM and Gf positively predicted trust recovery after automation failures, while AC influenced long-term trust calibration, with high-AC individuals showing more nuanced trust adjustments reflecting system reliability history. Trust decline was uniform across ability levels, suggesting that trust loss may occur rapidly after salient failures. The relationship between abilities and trust may have been partially mediated by automation schemas, with WM negatively correlating with all-or-none thinking about automation. These findings suggest different cognitive abilities play distinct roles in trust dynamics: WM supports monitoring automation performance, Gf enables effective schema updating, and AC facilitates appropriate deployment of these resources for trust calibration. This work advances our understanding of trust mechanisms and has implications for designing automation interfaces that accommodate individual cognitive differences.

items.title: Cognitive digital twins: A state-of-the-art review
items.abstract: Digital twin (DT), as a key enabling technology of Industry 4.0, have transformed real-time monitoring and simulation by offering digital representations of physical systems. However, the growing complexity of modern systems needs increasingly advanced capabilities that extend beyond replication. Cognitive Digital Twin (CDT) extend the capabilities of traditional DT by integrating cognitive functions such as perception, attention, memory, reasoning, problem solving and learning through artificial intelligence (AI) techniques such as machine learning (ML). Despite the lack of literature due to the field's infancy, CDT is becoming key tools for Industry 4.0/5.0, making systems more autonomous and adaptable. This research explores CDT developments, their differences from traditional DT, and how they operationalize cognitive functions. We investigate CDT technologies through quantitative and qualitative assessments, emphasizing particular algorithms, software, tools, and frameworks across various sectors. The review identifies current advancements, maps cognitive functions to CDT applications, and highlights critical gaps, establishing a foundation for future research.

items.title: Cognitive-Logical Concept for Operational Resilience of Cyber-Physical Infrastructure: Decision-Making by a “Human-Agent” System Under Critical Threats
items.abstract: The paper substantiates the factors that give rise to crisis situations and conflicts during the management of energy-active facilities – situations that frequently escalate into emergencies requiring rapid response and effective decision-making. In such contexts, it is crucial to examine the psychological and intellectual resilience of operators, as this resilience underpins the capacity of systems and agents to function within the scope of defined objectives and authorities. Such resilience serves as a key factor in maintaining functional efficiency when countering various types of threats and attacks. A significant aspect of functional resilience involves analysing the logic behind decision-making aimed at achieving system-oriented outcomes. These decisions are grounded in principles of coherence, multi-level analysis, and risk assessment. Identifying the structure of this management logic and the associated decision-making procedures enables the development of efficient algorithms for addressing crisis situations – algorithms applicable across diverse fields, ranging from security management to socio-economic systems. The challenge of making efficient decisions – whether by an intelligent agent (a team player), an operational team, or a managerial/administrative structure – is determined by a complex interplay of psycho-neurophysiological and intellectual factors, operating at both the individual and team levels. They are participants in a game structure that shapes the strategy of permissible actions. To address this problem, the paper develops a cognitive-logical concept for the operational resilience of cyber-physical infrastructure, which integrates a “human-agent” into a unified situational control loop. Based on the category algebra, a category-theoretic information model is constructed for the decomposition of a hierarchical production structure, accounting for 16 threat-resilient personnel levels (P1–P16). By integrating H. Gardner’s theory of multiple intelligences and R. Sternberg’s triarchic theory, a cognitive map for operator decision-making during laser-based environmental monitoring is formalized. A mathematical framework for the quantitative assessment of personnel actions is developed, incorporating cognitive coefficients (KF), confidence levels (K(B)), and error risk factors (Ri). Practical testing of the system at the Burshtyn Power Station (Ukraine) and glass-manufacturing companies has demonstrated its efficiency under extreme operating conditions (1200°C–1500°C). Implementation of this method has reduced the reaction time of operational and dispatch personnel during pre-emergency and emergency conditions (Alarm/Avaria) and minimized the overall risk of error decisions stemming from the human factor.

items.title: Comparative Performance of Dental Students on Two Virtual Reality Simulators: A Crossover Study With Simodont and Virteasy
items.abstract: PURPOSE: This study aimed to explore the convergent validity of two widely used virtual reality (VR) haptic dental simulators, Simodont and Virteasy, by comparing dental students' performance on comparable abstract psychomotor tasks. Secondary objectives were to examine short-term learning effects, simulator order, and the potential influence of additional clinical exposure. METHODS: A two-period crossover study was conducted with 74 fourth-year dental students corresponding to 222 paired exercise datasets. Each participant completed three progressively complex tasks (direct line, indirect line, indirect cross) on both simulators, 6 months apart. Primary outcome measures were the percentage of target removed on Simodont and the percentage of progression achieved on Virteasy. Secondary outcomes included simulator-specific scores, drill time, and total task time. Paired t-tests and within-subject comparisons were used for analysis. RESULTS: Differences were observed between simulators for target-related metrics and drill time outcomes. Virteasy generated higher target progression values, whereas longer drill times were recorded on this platform. Given the substantial differences in scoring logic, ergonomics, and workflow implementation between systems, these metrics should not be interpreted as indicators of simulator efficiency or learner superiority. No significant period effect was observed (+0.6%, p = 0.36). Both simulators demonstrated short-term learning effects, with the greatest improvement between the first and second attempts. Simulator order had no significant influence on performance. Precision on Virteasy did not correlate with Simodont composite scores. CONCLUSIONS: Both simulators supported effective psychomotor task execution but produced non-equivalent performance outcomes due to differences in feedback, ergonomics, and scoring logic. These findings support the view that Simodont and Virteasy assess partially overlapping constructs rather than interchangeable competencies. Future research should focus on mapping simulator-specific metrics to defined competency frameworks rather than harmonizing scores across platforms.

items.title: Compile Away Uncertainty: Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Programmatic Compilation
items.abstract: Self-evolving agent skills enable AI agents to accumulate and refine reusable procedural knowledge from interaction experience without updating model parameters. However, since such skills are typically represented as textual documents and executed through LLM reasoning, even previously learned procedures must be repeatedly interpreted and regenerated, introducing avoidable uncertainty into every execution. In contrast, program execution is deterministic and independently verifiable. Intuitively, transforming well-specified operations into executable programs can reduce reliance on LLM reasoning and, consequently, reduce execution uncertainty. Motivated by this intuition, we introduce SKillCompiler, a self-evolving skill framework that integrates programmatic compilation into the skill evolution process. Specifically, SkillCompiler adopts an executability-aware skill compilation strategy that decomposes skills into fine-grained operations, analyzes their executability, and constructs hybrid skill skeletons that retain LLM reasoning for context-dependent operations while compiling well-specified ones into validated programs. To avoid redundant program synthesis and enable executable knowledge to accumulate across evolving skills, we further design a program asset reuse mechanism that organizes validated programs as reusable assets, retrieves existing implementations whenever applicable, and synthesizes and verifies new programs only when necessary. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks and six model families demonstrate that SkillCompiler consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving up to 32.33\% improvement in task performance.

items.title: Compliance by Design: Governing AI ‐Augmented Quantitative Analysis in Clinical and Translational Research
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from promise to routine practice in clinical and translational research, and large language models (LLMs) are now used to scope analyses, draft and debug code, and accelerate the quantitative work that supports clinical and translational decisions. This adoption is outpacing the operational safeguards that keep such work reproducible and auditable, and the central risk is not only erroneous code but the quieter erosion of the analytical discipline on which trustworthy bench‐to‐bedside decisions depend. In this position paper, we argue that AI can be integrated into regulated quantitative workflows without sacrificing reproducibility, provided it operates inside a compliance‐by‐design architecture built on two principles: analytical intent must be formally encoded and locked before execution, and the analysis itself must run outside the LLM as specification‐verified code in a validated environment. We describe three failure modes that ordinary quality control does not detect, namely context drift, the displacement effect, and implementation drift, and we link each to documented model behavior. For open‐ended investigation, these principles are operationalized as a four‐step execution firewall; for recurring development studies such as assay validations and animal safety studies, they are operationalized through a governed library of documented, validated agents, supported by fit‐for‐purpose validation, a clear separation of human and machine roles, and post‐deployment monitoring. Both approaches can be implemented with components available today. Used this way, AI enhances rather than replaces quantitative expertise, which now resides less in the code a model produces than in the constraints a scientist defines before it runs.

items.title: Compliance with Occupational Health and Safety Requirements in Uganda's Construction Sector: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Construction is a high-risk industry and in Uganda it is regulated by the Occupational safety and Health Act, 2006. However, there is limited evidence on how well construction employers comply with their legal duties and why. This evidence gap has also not been reviewed. To identify, appraise and synthesize the evidence on compliance with occupational health and safety (OHS) requirements in Uganda's construction sector, the determinants of compliance and the regulatory and enforcement environment. The review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020. CORE (3 searches), Consensus and Google Scholar were searched and records imported into Zotero on 22 October 2026. A total of 226 records were identified, of which 157 unique records were screened. 8 reports out of 13 requested were assessed for eligibility. Studies were eligible if they investigated compliance, practices, injuries or regulation of OHS in Uganda's construction sector. We evaluated quality with a six-domain instrument. Results were thematically synthesized. Six studies from 2016 to 2023 were included: four cross-sectional or case studies, one regulatory review with key informant interviews and one master's thesis. Five themes emerged: the level of compliance and its measurement, organizational rather than personal determinants of compliance, outdated law and limited enforcement capacity, personal protective equipment as the most visible gap, differences between building and road sites and between firms. One study reported 95% compliance that its own scale classed as unacceptable and another reported an injury prevalence of 32.4%. No included study analyses inspection or prosecution data, or the construction-specific duties of employers under the 2006 Act. Compliance in Uganda's construction sector appears to be partial and organization-driven, with a regulatory framework described as outdated and weakly enforced. The evidence is limited, focused on Kampala and mainly cross-sectional. Five relevant reports could not be obtained. The priority areas include enforcement data, doctrinal analysis of employer duties and studies of small contractors and sites outside Kampala.

items.title: Computing with Coupled Oscillator Networks: Optimization, Memory, and Modern AI Primitives
items.abstract: We explore how synchronization in coupled oscillator networks may be employed to perform a variety of computing tasks. These systems are becoming more attractive as an alternative to conventional digital computers due to the increasing energy demands of the latter, particularly for large-scale problems in machine learning and artificial intelligence. The ubiquity of coupled oscillator networks means that oscillator-based computing can be thought of as a universal computing paradigm encompassing systems with a diversity of physical realizations, e.g. as analog circuits, neurological systems, spintronic systems. The bridge between the dynamics of coupled oscillator networks and computational primitives they implement is the Ising model, which originates in statistical physics, and when applied to oscillator networks, explains the emergence of globally complex and disordered synchronization patterns from local interactions in the network. We discuss the application of coupled oscillator networks to three fundamental computing operations. First, oscillator networks as specialized hardware solvers of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, with the solution encoded in the synchrony patterns. Second, oscillator networks as associative memory systems, enabling storage and retrieval of data represented through phases of oscillations. Finally, oscillator networks as a dynamical implementation of attention, with synchronization providing the mechanism for the alignment of keys to queries. The ability of oscillator networks to implement these computational primitives paves the way for novel realizations of intelligent systems through a variety of physical substrates.

items.title: Confidence-Modulated Safety Filtering for End-to-End Policies
items.abstract: End-to-end policies, from task-specific controllers to robot foundation models, learn complex behavior from raw observations but are not guaranteed to remain safe, so they are often wrapped in a safety filter. The resulting system operates under two domains: the filter's operational design domain (ODD), where its assumptions hold and safety is certified, and the policy's competence domain, where it is reliable. Filters typically fix their conservativeness regardless of the policy's competence, trading performance inside the ODD against margin beyond it. We ask whether the policy's confidence should set that level, and propose a filter-agnostic pipeline that modulates it at runtime: inside the ODD, where every setting is safe, confidence buys performance; beyond it, low confidence adds margin, which helps when it flags where the filter's model fails. Preliminary F1TENTH simulations, where this holds, show the modulated filter combining the strengths of permissive and conservative filters.

items.title: Conscience in the Age of Algorithms: Ethical Dilemmas in Generative AI Use Across Faith-Based Higher Education Institutions
items.abstract: This study explored the ethical tensions and dilemmas emerging across stakeholder groups- research administrators, faculty, and undergraduate students- regarding the use of Generative AI in academic research within faith-based higher education institutions in Mindanao, Philippines. A qualitative, holistic multiple-case study design was employed across five institutions, with fifteen participants (one administrator, one faculty member, and one student per institution) selected through purposive maximum variation sampling; semi-structured interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis for within-case analysis and Merriam’s five-step approach for cross-case synthesis. Nine essential themes emerged, three per stakeholder group, reflecting dilemmas of efficiency versus authentic learning, detection versus procedural fairness, innovation versus institutional integrity, assistance versus intellectual dependency, accuracy versus fabrication, professional judgment versus consistency, convenience versus genuine learning, confidence versus guilt and fear, and reliable detection versus equitable access to support, with institutional capacity emerging as a significant mediating factor that shaped both policy formalization and enforcement consistency. In addressing a contextual gap left by secular-focused studies, this research also fills a methodological gap: prior Philippine studies on faith-based AI governance relied largely on document analysis, whereas this study uses semi-structured interviews across three stakeholder groups within each institution, capturing lived experiences of ethical decision-making. The findings provide empirical evidence of how faith-based Philippine institutions navigate Gen AI ethical dilemmas and inform institutional policy design, faculty development, reform of detection practices, and student support mechanisms, particularly in resource-limited settings where ethical governance must be adapted to available capacity.

items.title: Construct Validity of Frontier Large Language Models on 4 Spanish Health Professions Specialty-Access Examinations (MIR, EIR, PIR, and FIR): Cross-Sectional Benchmarking and Psychometric Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) achieve high scores on health-professions examinations. Whether these scores support the same interpretations as human scores remains uncertain. Spain uses parallel multiple-choice examinations for entry to specialty training in medicine (Médico Interno Residente [MIR]), nursing (Enfermero Interno Residente [EIR]), psychology (Psicólogo Interno Residente [PIR]), and pharmacy (Farmacéutico Interno Residente [FIR]). Objective Using the January 2026 MIR, EIR, PIR, and FIR examinations, this study aimed to quantify the correspondence between human and LLM item facility and to describe model accuracy, distractor selection, and performance associated with measured surface features. Methods We evaluated 839 valid items using 12 configurations: GPT-5.2 at 3 reasoning efforts and Claude Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 4.5 (Anthropic), each under neutral and expert prompts, with one run per configuration. The primary measure was the Spearman correlation (ρ) between human and machine facility on 828 complete paired items. We examined sensitivity to panel composition, scoring, pooling, and assumed reliability; compared distractor choices with a post hoc plausibility-weighted baseline; and evaluated a surface-feature classifier. Image analyses distinguished supplied from withheld images. An exploratory LLM-judge audit assessed generated explanations. Bootstrap CIs resample items or, for distractor concordance, error events; they exclude run-to-run uncertainty. Results The highest pooled accuracy was 94.8% (795/839); all 12 configurations answered 668 of 828 paired items correctly (80.7%). Scores clustered near the ceiling among the strongest configurations. Human and machine facility correlated at 0.40 (95% CI 0.34-0.45), with estimates of 0.31 to 0.40 across panel definitions and 0.39 (95% CI 0.33-0.45) after exam-stratified pooling. The observed correlation was lower than predicted by a specified one-axis simulation with a uniform model advantage (0.63; predictive interval 0.59 to 0.66; P <.001). Among 672 model errors, dominant human-distractor selection differed from the plausibility-weighted baseline by –1.25 percentage points (95% CI –4.53 to 2.19), compatible with no difference. Surface-feature accuracy was 34.4% (289/839), similar to selecting the longest option (34.6%, 290/839). The adjusted association with model correctness was uncertain (odds ratio [OR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.72-1.04). Image-associated accuracy was lower both when images were supplied (OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.21-0.53) and when withheld (OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.08-0.16). Conclusions In this single 2026 cohort, high LLM scores coexisted with limited separation among the strongest configurations and moderate correspondence with human item difficulty. These findings caution against interpreting model scores as equivalent evidence of human competence. They do not establish clinical performance or invalidate the examinations for human candidates.

items.title: Consumers or Producers? The Feedback–Autonomy Paradox of AI Tools in Blended ESP Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools now reach English for Specific Purposes (ESP) students through the smartphones they already carry, often before institutions have decided how these tools should be used. This qualitative case study examines how ESP students and teachers at a university in the Sultanate of Oman experienced AI-supported feedback in blended learning, and how the appeal of immediate feedback interacted with the need for learner autonomy. The data come from a wider doctoral study of mobile technology in ESP classes and comprise semi-structured interviews with ESP teachers, five focus groups with 30 second-year students from maritime, engineering and medical programmes, 81 open-ended questionnaire responses and three classroom observations. AI use was not a preset topic; it emerged from participants’ own accounts of the applications they used. Students described ChatGPT and AI speaking applications as an always-available, non-judgmental tutor that gave immediate feedback and helped them rehearse speaking, writing and professional communication with more confidence. Teachers welcomed this but worried that students might become consumers rather than producers of language. We interpret these accounts as a feedback–autonomy paradox: the support that builds confidence can also crowd out independent effort, while autonomy without guidance leaves learners unsure of their progress. Teachers managed the paradox through dialogical use of AI, recorded practice followed by peer or teacher feedback, and professionally authentic tasks, while cost, limited training and the absence of shared guidance constrained equitable access. We argue that the feedback–autonomy balance should be treated as a design decision that changes over the course of a programme, and we outline implications for ESP teachers and institutions.

items.title: Creativity and Its Related Factors
items.abstract: Creativity is an essential human ability that contributes to intellectual development, innovation, problem-solving, and social progress. In contemporary society, creativity has gained considerable importance in education, science, technology, business, and everyday life. It enables individuals to generate original ideas, explore alternative solutions, and respond effectively to emerging challenges. However, creativity is not determined by a single ability or personality characteristic. It develops through the interaction of psychological, cognitive, social, cultural, and educational factors. The present article examines the concept of creativity and analyses the major factors associated with its development and expression. Particular attention is given to intelligence, divergent thinking, motivation, personality, emotional intelligence, self-efficacy, family environment, peer relationships, cultural influences, educational practices, and institutional climate. The study adopts descriptive approach based on a review of relevant literature. The analysis suggests that creativity is best understood as a multidimensional and context-sensitive phenomenon involving both individual potential and environmental opportunities. Supportive social relationships, intrinsic motivation, intellectual freedom, and learner-centered educational practices can encourage creative expression, whereas excessive control, fear of failure, and rigid assessment practices may restrict it. The article concludes that creativity can be nurtured through appropriate educational experiences, reflective thinking, collaboration, and opportunities for experimentation.

items.title: Critical AI literacy as a buffer against AI overtrust in students
items.abstract: Abstract Background The increasing adoption of AI tools such as ChatGPT in academic contexts has introduced a new psychological risk: overtrust in AI. However, the psychological foundations and boundary conditions of AI overtrust remain insufficiently examined. This study examined how self-efficacy, intrinsic motivation, and extrinsic motivation influence AI overtrust, and whether AI literacy can mitigate its negative consequences. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 300 university students in South Korea who had prior academic experience using AI tools. The questionnaire measured academic self-efficacy, intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, AI literacy, and AI overtrust. Structural equation modeling was used to test direct and mediated effects among the variables, with bootstrapping employed to evaluate indirect pathways. Results Self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation were positively associated with AI overtrust, suggesting that learners with higher confidence and autonomy exhibit overtrust in AI-generated information. Extrinsic motivation showed a weaker direct effect. AI literacy had a significant negative effect on AI overtrust and mediated the relationship between both self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation and overtrust. A sequential mediation model indicated that performance expectation and AI literacy together suppressed overtrust by strengthening reflective awareness. Conclusions These findings demonstrate that high-performing and intrinsically motivated learners are psychologically vulnerable to AI overtrust. Although high academic self-efficacy fosters autonomy in using AI tools, it also increases the risk of overtrust in AI. Targeted AI literacy education addresses this risk by enhancing learners’ critical thinking, ethical awareness, and responsible AI use. AI literacy education should be adapted to learners’ psychological profiles to effectively prevent AI overtrust and support responsible use.

items.title: Cross-Tissue Mining of Shared Molecular Pathways and Cell-State Programs in Chronic Pain and Psychiatric Comorbidity: An Agentic, Benchmarked, Reproducible Target-Nomination Pipeline — Analysis Plan (public preregistration, v2; not peer-reviewed)
items.abstract: 2-1. Abstract Chronic pain frequently co-occurs with depression and anxiety, and a shared low-grade inflammatory / neuroimmune substrate has been repeatedly proposed. This project asks which molecular pathways and cell-state programs are shared across the two conditions, and which of those are druggable or repurposable. Design. This is an entirely in-silico, secondary-data study using public resources only (PubMed / PMC OA, Open Targets, HGNC, NCBI gene2pubmed, public bulk and single-nucleus RNA-seq, and GWAS). An LLM multi-agent pipeline (driven by Anthropic Claude) mines a citation-verified literature corpus, builds a cross-database target map (UniProt / Reactome / ChEMBL / GEO / ClinVar), re-analyses pain-side (human peripheral nerve, bulk RNA-seq) and psychiatric-side (human cortex, single-nucleus) expression data for direction-concordance, and emits a single ranking over the protein-coding gene universe. In the primary analysis, both sides of the expression comparison are human. The pain side is human peripheral nerve (Morton's neuroma resected for pain, and control nerves), not dorsal root ganglion (where the neuronal cell bodies are). Because we found no public human data comparing dorsal root ganglia with and without pain, a mouse dorsal root ganglion nerve-injury model is used as a sensitivity analysis. In that sensitivity analysis, mouse genes are first mapped to their human counterparts (one-to-one orthologs) before the direction of change is compared; this mapping is needed only in the sensitivity analysis, where the two sides differ in species. Genes without a one-to-one counterpart drop out of that comparison, and changes in a mouse nerve-injury model are not guaranteed to match those in human chronic pain. On the primary-analysis pain side, group and sex are imbalanced (the neuroma group is mostly female), so sex is included as a covariate. We state these as limitations. Blinding is impossible: a single PI develops, runs and reports the analysis. Procedural controls (a fixed calendar freeze date, capped evaluation runs, frozen code hashes, full deposition of logs) replace blinding and are described explicitly, including their limits. Note on the word "reproducible" in the title: it refers to the evaluation stage (frozen ranking CSV -> frozen metric code -> reported numbers), not to re-execution of the generative pipeline, whose LLM agents are not deterministic. Confirmatory vs exploratory. Only one part of this project is confirmatory: whether the pipeline recovers a set of 20 held-out, previously known shared targets at higher recall@k (k = 50 and 100, both fixed in advance) than a frozen Open Targets baseline (dataVersion 26.06, frozen 2026-08-11). Everything else — the newly nominated targets outside the held-out set and their biological interpretation — is exploratory and has NOT been experimentally validated. The rigour of the confirmatory benchmark does not transfer to the nominated targets. Relation to prior work. Multi-agent LLM systems for therapeutic hypothesis generation and target discovery, citation-verifying literature agents, and benchmarking of LLM target rankings against Open Targets by top-K recovery of known targets have all been reported previously. In particular, TargetBench 1.0 has already compared a panel of LLMs — including Claude-Opus-4 — against Open Targets by how many known clinical-stage targets they recover in their top K (precision at top K) over an HGNC protein-coding gene universe of comparable size to the one used here. This project does not claim any of these as new. Its increments are (i) the controlled conditions — a publicly registered analysis plan fixed before any ranking is generated, a deny-list of the evidence sources behind the held-out set whose identifiers are published in full after the freeze, exact inference, and a stopping rule — and (ii) the application domain, the pain-psychiatry comorbid pair (a co-occurring pair of conditions rather than a single disease) evaluated across peripheral and central tissue (in the primary analysis, human peripheral nerve from Morton's neuroma on the pain side and human cerebral cortex from patients with major depressive disorder on the psychiatric side; in a sensitivity analysis, the pain side is replaced by mouse DRG in a nerve-injury model, linked by one-to-one orthologs). Limits stated up front. Isolation from an LLM's pre-training corpus is impossible in principle. "Held-out" here means held out from the pipeline-construction corpus only, so the claim is calibration of reconstruction from public information, not prediction of unknown biology. Because the 20 targets are among the most-studied molecules in the field, recall@k may partly measure literature prominence; a PubMed co-occurrence ranking is therefore registered as a third baseline and will be reported alongside the main result regardless of outcome. Whether this baseline is available for the main analysis is fixed in advance by a pre-committed rule that does not depend on when it is implemented: if the script eval/pubmed_cooccurrence_baseline.py and its outputs do not exist at the time the freeze procedure is completed, we will under no circumstance claim to outperform "existing approaches"; the claim will be restricted to outperforming Open Targets, and the statement that recall@k may be explained by literature prominence will be placed in both the Abstract and the Discussion - that is, the same treatment as if the co-occurrence baseline had not been outperformed. The failure to implement will be recorded as a deviation. The rule is mechanical: no discretion is exercised at the freeze date. Isolation is implemented, not merely declared: the pipeline filters both the search stage and the full-text retrieval stage against a frozen deny-list, and records every document it did retrieve in out/retrieved_manifest.jsonl. The verification we will report is the intersection of the retrieved-identifier set with the deny-list; it will be reported even if it is empty, and any non-empty intersection will be reported in full as a deviation without rebuilding the ranking. We verify this only to the extent that it is mechanically detectable, and we do not claim completeness. Blocking sits on the corpus boundary rather than inside the retrieval tools: the scoring code reads only the gated corpus and aborts if any record lacks the gate's stamp, so material obtained outside the gate cannot enter the score. We do not claim that it cannot be read -- detection of that case rests on the contamination audit, which we report whatever it finds. This is a public preregistration. It has not undergone peer review and is not a Registered Report. 2-2. Status of the blocking mechanism The blocking mechanism and the retrieval manifest have been implemented (implementation was completed on 2026-10-09). The implementation consists of eval/denylist_filter.py (the blocking itself) and pipeline/retrieval_gate.py (the sole entry point to the evidence corpus). In testing, the blocking-mechanism tests pass 7/7 and the retrieval-gate tests pass 17/17, so all items pass (none of these tests requires a network connection; the retrieval-gate tests include cumulative counts, matching on all identifiers of a record, and re-matching of the corpus against the deny-list). The SHA-256 hashes of these files are given in §10-1. Claude Science is shown not the repository but only a dedicated folder that contains not a single file naming a gold target (the folder is created by pipeline/build_agent_view.py; the deny-list is placed in it with its identifier lines only, and all annotations, including which gold target each source supports, are removed). Details of the relation to prior work are given in §4-4 "Relation to prior work".

items.title: CXRG-SVLM: a parameter-efficient small vision-language model for multi-view chest X-ray report generation in resource-constrained environments
items.abstract: Abstract Automated chest X-ray report generation reduces reporting delays in resource-constrained clinical environments. Existing vision-language models often rely on large language models or full fine-tuning. This dependence causes high computational costs and limits on-premise deployment. We propose CXRG-SVLM. This small vision-language model combines a frozen RAD-DINO medical image encoder with a 4-bit quantized Qwen2.5-3B language model adapted using 4-bit QLoRA. A multi-view fusion module integrates frontal and lateral radiographs into a compact continuous visual representation. The resulting visual tokens are projected into the language-model embedding space and concatenated with clinical-indication embeddings to form a conditioning prefix. The decoder uses its native causal self-attention over this prefix and the generated tokens to produce the Findings report. The assembled implementation reports approximately 1.99 billion loaded parameter elements, of which approximately 38.1 million are trainable, corresponding to 1.91% of this framework-reported inventory. We evaluated the model on the Indiana University Chest X-ray dataset to generate the Findings section of the radiology report. The proposed model attains a ROUGE-L score of 0.3527 and a METEOR score of 0.2744. Automated entity-level agreement varies across findings, with the strongest F1 for normal descriptors and measurable agreement for pleural effusion, pneumothorax, and mediastinal mentions under the reported rule-based evaluation. Efficiency testing shows an average generation time of 5.27 seconds per report on a single graphics processing unit. These results establish the model’s computational feasibility and motivate subsequent radiologist evaluation of factual correctness, safety, and practical usefulness. Ultimately, CXRG-SVLM demonstrates that a parameter-efficient approach with less than 2% trainable parameters maintains competitive semantic fidelity, establishing an accessible foundation for future, prospectively validated on-premise clinical decision-support tools.

items.title: Deriving Metacognitive Scaffolding Design Principles and an Integrated Model for Generative AI–Supported Major Exploration
items.abstract: As flexible major selection systems, including undeclared admission, become increasingly widespread in higher education, learners' capacity for self-directed academic and career planning has become more important than ever.Although the widespread adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) has improved the efficiency of information acquisition, it also raises concerns about intensified cognitive offloading, whereby learners become overly dependent on AI-generated responses without engaging in critical thinking.To address this issue, this study proposes an AI-based integrated metacognitive scaffolding model that enables learners to use AI not merely as an information provider, but as a tool for expanding their thinking.To this end, an integrative literature review explored the theoretical relationship between metacognition and scaffolding, and a cross-mapping analysis was used to derive stage-specific design principles.In addition, a scenario-based walkthrough examined the logical applicability of the proposed model.The analysis suggests that AI-supported major exploration can be conceptually organized around the role of an Inquiring Coach.The proposed model organizes the learning process into three metacognitive phases-Planning, Monitoring, and Evaluation-and specifies stage-specific strategies, including delaying immediate answers, detecting inconsistencies and generating counter-questions, and promoting reflective self-explanation.The model also incorporates a Fading mechanism as a design principle intended to support the gradual development of learners' selfdirected exploration.This study provides conceptual design guidelines for AI-supported career education systems.It proposes a theoretical basis for shifting attention from information-delivery efficiency to designing interactions that support learners' thinking.However, the model's effects on learners' metacognition or career decision-making were not empirically tested.

items.title: Design and Field Validation of a VR-Based RAG Historical NPC: Knowledge Grounding and Persona Grounding Can Fail Independently
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based non-player characters (NPCs) can support unscripted historical dialogue, but their behavior in deployed educational virtual reality (VR) settings remains underexamined. This study reports the design and field validation of a self-hosted VR platform in which a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) NPC, representing King Sejong the Great, engaged 42 international participants across 126 intercultural-learning sessions. The analytic corpus, reconstructed from retained session logs, comprised 104 sessions from 39 participants (2053 participant turns; 2053 NPC responses). Repetitive NPC response loops occurred in 33 sessions (31.7%), spanning 54 episodes and 190 responses, and co-occurred with learner-side transcript repetition in 31 of these sessions. The NPC maintained its first-person persona throughout the screened corpus, yet produced 30 biographical claims unsupported by the historical record: persona consistency did not ensure factual grounding. Prompt compliance varied by instruction type, and a post hoc implementation audit could not confirm that retrieved content contributed to individual responses. Together, these results identify persona grounding, knowledge grounding, retrieval observability, and session-level instrumentation as validation targets that deployed VR–LLM systems must address separately.
